decks.title: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter — Part 1: The photoelectric effect and photons
goals: Describe Hertz’s and Lenard’s observations and how photocurrent depends on intensity, frequency and collector potential
Explain why the wave theory of light fails to explain the photoelectric effect
Use Einstein’s equation K_max = hf − W₀ to find maximum kinetic energy, stopping potential, threshold frequency and threshold wavelength

slides.narration: By the end of the nineteenth century light was firmly a wave: it interferes, diffracts and is polarised. Then a set of simple experiments showed light knocking electrons out of metal surfaces in a way no wave could. In this part we look at those experiments, see exactly where the wave theory breaks down, and meet Einstein’s explanation in terms of packets of light energy called photons.

slides.heading: Hertz’s observation (1887)
slides.body_md: While producing radio waves with a spark gap, Hertz noticed that sparks jumped across the small **receiver gap** more readily when **ultraviolet light** from the transmitter spark fell on it.
bullets: A glass sheet in between (glass absorbs ultraviolet) made the receiver sparks shorter; a quartz sheet (transparent to ultraviolet) did not.
Hallwachs then found that a negatively charged zinc plate in ultraviolet light loses its charge: light frees **negative** charges from metals.
These charges were later shown to be electrons: **photoelectrons**.

slides.narration: Hertz was studying radio waves made by a spark across a gap. He noticed that a small receiver gap sparked more easily when ultraviolet light from the main spark reached it. A sheet of glass, which absorbs ultraviolet, weakened the effect; quartz, which lets it through, did not. Soon after, it was found that ultraviolet light makes a negatively charged zinc plate lose its charge. Light was freeing electrons from metals.

slides.heading: Lenard’s apparatus
slides.body_md: An evacuated bulb holds an **emitter** C and a **collector** A. Monochromatic light enters through a **quartz window** (it passes ultraviolet) and falls on C. A battery across a rheostat with a **reversing key** sets the potential V of A relative to C; a microammeter reads the **photocurrent**.
bullets: The vacuum lets electrons reach A without colliding with gas molecules.
A positive: A attracts the electrons. A negative: A repels them (a **retarding** potential).

slides.narration: Lenard sealed two metal plates in an evacuated bulb. Light of a single frequency enters through a quartz window and falls on the emitter. Electrons freed from it travel to the collector, and the microammeter reads the resulting photocurrent. A potential divider and a reversing key let him make the collector either positive, to attract the electrons, or negative, to push them back.

slides.heading: Photocurrent, intensity and potential
slides.body_md: Keep the frequency fixed (above threshold) and vary the collector potential V:
bullets: Even at V = 0 a current flows: the electrons leave C with kinetic energy.
As V is made positive, the current rises to a **saturation** value, when every emitted electron is collected. Saturation current ∝ intensity.
As V is made negative, the current falls; it is zero at $V = -V_0$, the **stopping potential**: $eV_0 = K_{\max}$.
V₀ is the same for every intensity.

visual.alt: Graph of photocurrent against collector potential for 412.5 nanometre light on barium at three intensities: each curve is zero below minus 0.5 volt, rises as the collector becomes less negative and then levels off; the level is proportional to the intensity, but all three curves start from the same stopping potential
visual.caption: One frequency, three intensities: saturation current ∝ intensity; stopping potential unchanged.

slides.narration: With light of one frequency, a current flows even with no voltage, because the electrons leave the emitter with some kinetic energy. Making the collector positive gathers more of them until every emitted electron is collected: the current saturates, and the saturation current is proportional to the intensity. Making the collector negative turns electrons back, and at the stopping potential even the fastest are stopped. Notice that the stopping potential is the same for all three intensities.

slides.heading: The effect of frequency
slides.body_md: Now keep the number of photons per second fixed and change the frequency f:
bullets: The **stopping potential rises with frequency**: the fastest electrons are faster.
The saturation current is unchanged: the same number of electrons is freed each second.
Below a **threshold frequency** f₀, characteristic of the metal, there is **no current at all**, however intense the light.

visual.alt: Graph of photocurrent against collector potential for barium lit by three frequencies with the same number of photons per second: the three curves level off at the same saturation current, but the higher the frequency, the more negative the potential needed to stop the current, 0.5, 1.25 and 2.0 volts
visual.caption: Same photon rate, three frequencies: same saturation current; higher frequency, larger stopping potential.

slides.narration: Now change the colour of the light while keeping the number of photons per second the same. The curves level off at the same saturation current, but a higher frequency needs a larger negative potential to stop the current, so the fastest electrons must be faster. And below a certain threshold frequency, which depends on the metal, no electrons come out at all, no matter how bright the light.

slides.heading: Why the wave theory fails
slides.body_md: In the wave theory, light energy is spread continuously over the wavefront and delivered at a rate set by the **intensity**. That predicts the opposite of three key facts:

rows: No emission below a threshold frequency f₀, however bright the light
Any frequency works if the light is bright enough
K_max (and V₀) rises with frequency, not with intensity
Emission starts at once (within about 10⁻⁹ s), even in dim light
A delay while each electron gathers energy

visual.alt: Table comparing four experimental facts of the photoelectric effect with what the wave theory of light expects: only the proportionality of the saturation current to intensity agrees

slides.narration: If light were only a wave, its energy would be spread evenly over the wavefront. A brighter beam would deliver energy faster, so electrons should come out faster, and any colour should work if it is bright enough, after a delay while energy builds up. Experiments show the opposite: a threshold frequency, a maximum kinetic energy set by the frequency alone, and no delay at all. Only the link between intensity and current agrees.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how long would a wave take?
slides.body_md: A 2.0 W lamp radiates uniformly in all directions. A barium surface (W₀ = 2.5 eV) is 1.5 m away. On the wave theory, an electron can collect energy only from an area of about 1.0 × 10⁻²⁰ m² (roughly one atom). Estimate how long it would need to gather 2.5 eV.
bullets: Intensity at 1.5 m: $I = \dfrac{P}{4\pi r^2} = \dfrac{2.0}{4\pi \times 1.5^2} \approx 0.0707$ W m⁻².
Power reaching one electron: $IA \approx 0.0707 \times 1.0 \times 10^{-20} = 7.07 \times 10^{-22}$ W.
Time: $t = \dfrac{2.5 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{7.07 \times 10^{-22}} \approx 565$ s, about 9 minutes. Experiment: emission within about $10^{-9}$ s.

visual.alt: Table of the wave-theory estimate: intensity, power reaching one electron, the predicted delay of about nine minutes, and the observed delay of under a nanosecond

slides.narration: The lamp’s two watts spread over a sphere of radius one and a half metres, giving about seven hundredths of a watt per square metre. An area the size of an atom then receives only about seven times ten to the minus twenty two watts. Gathering two and a half electronvolts would take over nine minutes. In reality the electrons appear within a billionth of a second.

slides.heading: Quantisation of radiation: photons
slides.body_md:
Planck (1900) had found that the radiation from hot bodies is emitted in packets of energy $hf$. **Einstein (1905)** went further: light itself travels as packets, **photons**, each of energy
$$E = hf = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda},\qquad h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$$
bullets: Intensity = (number of photons per second per unit area) × hf.
A photon is absorbed whole, by one electron, or not at all.
Useful: $\dfrac{hc}{e} = 1237.5$ eV nm with these constants, so $E\,(\text{eV}) = \dfrac{1237.5}{\lambda\,(\text{nm})}$.

slides.narration: Planck had already shown that hot bodies emit radiation in packets of energy h f. Einstein proposed that light itself travels in such packets, called photons. Each photon carries energy h f, or h c over lambda, where h is Planck’s constant. A brighter beam means more photons, not bigger ones. And a photon is absorbed whole, by a single electron.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting photons
slides.body_md: A blue-violet LED gives a 6.0 mW beam of wavelength 412.5 nm. Find the energy of each photon, in J and eV, its frequency, and the number of photons emitted per second.
bullets: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{412.5 \times 10^{-9}} = 4.8 \times 10^{-19}$ J $= 3.0$ eV.
$f = \dfrac{c}{\lambda} \approx 7.27 \times 10^{14}$ Hz.
$N = \dfrac{P}{E} = \dfrac{6.0 \times 10^{-3}}{4.8 \times 10^{-19}} = 1.25 \times 10^{16}$ photons per second.

visual.caption: Shorter wavelength, more energetic photons. Only photons above the dashed line can free electrons from barium.

slides.narration: Each photon carries h c over lambda, which is four point eight times ten to the minus nineteen joule, or exactly three electronvolts. The frequency is about seven point two seven times ten to the fourteen hertz. Dividing the power, six milliwatts, by the energy of one photon gives one point two five times ten to the sixteen photons every second: even a small LED emits an enormous number.

slides.heading: Einstein’s photoelectric equation
slides.body_md:
An electron at the top of the filled levels needs at least the **work function** $W_0$ to escape. It absorbs one photon; whatever is left becomes kinetic energy. Electrons from deeper levels leave with less, so
$$K_{\max} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_{\max}^2 = hf - W_0 = eV_0$$
bullets: **Threshold:** $K_{\max} = 0$ when $hf_0 = W_0$, so $f_0 = \dfrac{W_0}{h}$ and $\lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{W_0}$.
No emission if f < f₀ (λ > λ₀).

slides.narration: Picture the electrons in a metal filling energy levels up to a top level. To escape, an electron from the top must gain at least the work function. If a photon gives it h f, it leaves with h f minus the work function as kinetic energy. Electrons from deeper levels use up more energy on the way out, so this is the maximum kinetic energy. At the threshold frequency the photon has just enough energy to free an electron.

slides.heading: Work function and threshold
slides.body_md: The work function depends on the metal and the state of its surface. Alkali and alkaline-earth metals have small $W_0$ and respond to visible light; most others need ultraviolet. $\lambda_0\,(\text{nm}) = \dfrac{1237.5}{W_0\,(\text{eV})}$.

slides.narration: Each metal has its own work function, a few electronvolts, and so its own threshold wavelength. Rubidium, barium and strontium respond to visible light, because their thresholds lie in the visible range. Magnesium, tungsten, copper and platinum need ultraviolet. A clean surface and a dirty or oxidised one can differ, so tables give typical values.

slides.narration: Each photon carries one thousand two hundred and thirty seven point five divided by two hundred and twenty five, which is five point five electronvolts. Magnesium needs three point seven to release an electron, leaving one point eight electronvolts, so the stopping potential is one point eight volts and the fastest electrons move at about eight hundred kilometres per second. The threshold wavelength is about three hundred and thirty four nanometres.

slides.heading: Einstein’s equation explains the facts
slides.body_md: Writing $eV_0 = hf - W_0$ explains every observation in one line:
bullets: A graph of $K_{\max}$ against $f$ is a straight line of slope $h$, cutting the $f$ axis at $f_0$.

rows: A photon must bring at least W₀: hf₀ = W₀
Each electron takes one photon; intensity only changes the number of photons
A photon gives all its energy to one electron at once
More photons per second free more electrons per second

visual.alt: Table of how Einstein’s equation explains the threshold frequency, the dependence of maximum kinetic energy on frequency only, the absence of a time lag and the proportionality of current to intensity

slides.narration: Einstein’s equation explains all the facts at once. A photon must bring at least the work function, so there is a threshold. Each electron takes energy from a single photon, so the maximum kinetic energy depends on frequency, not intensity. The photon hands over its energy at once, so there is no delay. And a brighter beam carries more photons, freeing more electrons each second.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: how many photons free an electron?
slides.body_md: The 6.0 mW, 412.5 nm beam of example 2 falls on a barium emitter (W₀ = 2.5 eV). The saturation photocurrent is 9.6 μA. Find the stopping potential, the number of photoelectrons emitted per second and the fraction of photons that free an electron.
bullets: Electrons per second $= \dfrac{I}{e} = \dfrac{9.6 \times 10^{-6}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 6.0 \times 10^{13}$.
Fraction $= \dfrac{6.0 \times 10^{13}}{1.25 \times 10^{16}} = 4.8 \times 10^{-3}$: about one photon in 208 frees an electron.

visual.alt: Graph of photocurrent against collector potential for 412.5 nanometre light on barium at three intensities: each curve is zero below minus 0.5 volt, rises as the collector becomes less negative and then levels off; the level is proportional to the intensity, but all three curves start from the same stopping potential
visual.caption: One frequency, three intensities: saturation current ∝ intensity; stopping potential unchanged.

slides.narration: Each photon brings three electronvolts and barium needs two and a half, so the stopping potential is half a volt. A saturation current of nine point six microamperes means six times ten to the thirteen electrons per second. Compared with the photons arriving, that is only about one photon in two hundred: most photons are absorbed or reflected without freeing an electron.

goals: Find Planck’s constant and the work function from a graph of stopping potential against frequency

slides.heading: Planck’s Constant and Matter Waves
slides.body_md: Part 2 — measuring h from a straight-line graph, photons with momentum, and electrons that behave as waves.

visual.alt: Graph of stopping potential against frequency for barium and magnesium: two parallel straight lines, each starting on the frequency axis at that metal’s threshold frequency, about 6.06 and 8.97 times ten to the fourteen hertz, and rising with the same slope h over e, 0.4125 volt for every ten to the fourteen hertz
visual.caption: Same slope h/e for every metal; the line starts at the threshold frequency f₀ = W₀/h.

slides.narration: Einstein’s equation is easy to test: it predicts a straight-line graph whose slope contains Planck’s constant. We will use that graph to measure h. Then we see that photons carry momentum as well as energy, and finally meet de Broglie’s bold idea that electrons, and all matter, have waves too, an idea confirmed by Davisson and Germer.

slides.heading: Stopping potential against frequency
slides.body_md:
Divide Einstein’s equation by e:
$$V_0 = \dfrac{h}{e}\,f - \dfrac{W_0}{e}$$
A graph of $V_0$ against $f$ is a **straight line** with slope $\dfrac{h}{e}$, the same for **every** metal, cutting the $f$ axis at $f_0$.
bullets: With $h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34}$ J s the slope is $\dfrac{h}{e} = 4.125 \times 10^{-15}$ V s, that is 0.4125 V for every $10^{14}$ Hz.
Lines for different metals are parallel; a larger W₀ shifts the line to the right.

visual.alt: Graph of stopping potential against frequency for barium and magnesium: two parallel straight lines, each starting on the frequency axis at that metal’s threshold frequency, about 6.06 and 8.97 times ten to the fourteen hertz, and rising with the same slope h over e, 0.4125 volt for every ten to the fourteen hertz
visual.caption: Same slope h/e for every metal; the line starts at the threshold frequency f₀ = W₀/h.

slides.narration: Divide Einstein’s equation by the electronic charge. The stopping potential equals h over e times the frequency, minus the work function over e. So a graph of stopping potential against frequency is a straight line. Its slope, h over e, is a universal constant, so lines for different metals are parallel. Each line meets the frequency axis at that metal’s threshold frequency.

slides.heading: Reading h and W₀ from the graph
slides.body_md: From a measured line:
bullets: **Slope** $= \dfrac{\Delta V_0}{\Delta f} = \dfrac{h}{e}$, so $h = e \times \text{slope}$.
**Intercept on the f axis** $= f_0$, so $W_0 = hf_0$.
**Intercept on the $V_0$ axis** (extended back to $f = 0$) $= -\dfrac{W_0}{e}$.
Millikan did this carefully in 1916 and confirmed Einstein’s equation and the value of h.

visual.alt: Graph of stopping potential against frequency for barium and magnesium: two parallel straight lines, each starting on the frequency axis at that metal’s threshold frequency, about 6.06 and 8.97 times ten to the fourteen hertz, and rising with the same slope h over e, 0.4125 volt for every ten to the fourteen hertz
visual.caption: Same slope h/e for every metal; the line starts at the threshold frequency f₀ = W₀/h.

slides.narration: Measure the stopping potential at several frequencies and draw the best straight line. Its slope, multiplied by e, gives Planck’s constant. The point where it meets the frequency axis is the threshold frequency, and multiplying that by h gives the work function. Extended back to zero frequency, the line meets the potential axis at minus the work function over e. Millikan’s careful measurements of this kind confirmed Einstein’s equation.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: h from mercury lines
slides.body_md: A student lights a photocathode with four lines of a mercury lamp and records: 254 nm → 2.87 V; 313 nm → 1.95 V; 365 nm → 1.39 V; 405 nm → 1.06 V. Find h and the work function.
bullets: Frequencies $f = c/\lambda$: 11.8, 9.58, 8.22, 7.41 $\times 10^{14}$ Hz.
Slope (end points) $= \dfrac{2.87 - 1.06}{(11.8 - 7.41) \times 10^{14}} \approx 4.12 \times 10^{-15}$ V s, so $h = e \times \text{slope} \approx 6.60 \times 10^{-34}$ J s.
Intercept: $f_0 = 7.41 \times 10^{14} - \dfrac{1.06}{4.12 \times 10^{-15}} \approx 4.84 \times 10^{14}$ Hz; $W_0 = hf_0 \approx 2.0$ eV.

Its slope is about four point one two times ten to the minus fifteen volt seconds, and multiplying by e gives Planck’s constant, about six point six times ten to the minus thirty four joule seconds. The line meets the frequency axis near four point eight times ten to the fourteen hertz, giving a work function of about two electronvolts.

slides.heading: Photon momentum
slides.body_md:
A photon travels at c and has **zero rest mass**, yet it carries momentum. From relativity, for a particle with no rest mass $E = pc$, so
$$p = \dfrac{E}{c} = \dfrac{hf}{c} = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}$$
bullets: A beam absorbed by a surface pushes it: force = (photons per second) × h/λ = P/c.
Reflected straight back, each photon’s momentum is reversed: twice the force.
Solar sails and comet tails show light pressure.

visual.alt: Table of the properties of a photon: energy h f, momentum h over lambda, speed c, zero rest mass and zero charge

slides.narration: Photons have no rest mass, but they carry momentum: the photon’s energy divided by c, which equals h over lambda. Shorter wavelengths carry more momentum. When a beam is absorbed, its momentum is handed to the surface, which feels a tiny force equal to the beam power divided by c. If the beam is reflected straight back, the force doubles. This light pressure pushes comet tails away from the Sun.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: photon momentum and force
slides.body_md: A 2.0 mW green beam of wavelength 495 nm is completely absorbed by a black screen. Find the momentum of each photon, the number of photons arriving per second and the force on the screen.
bullets: $p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{495 \times 10^{-9}} \approx 1.33 \times 10^{-27}$ kg m s⁻¹.
$F = Np \approx 6.67 \times 10^{-12}$ N, the same as $\dfrac{P}{c} = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-3}}{3 \times 10^{8}}$.

visual.alt: Table of the properties of a photon: energy h f, momentum h over lambda, speed c, zero rest mass and zero charge

slides.narration: Each photon carries h over lambda, about one point three three times ten to the minus twenty seven kilogram metres per second. Each has two and a half electronvolts, so five times ten to the fifteen photons arrive every second. Their momentum per second is the force, about six point six seven times ten to the minus twelve newton, which is simply the power divided by the speed of light.

slides.heading: Wave–particle duality
slides.body_md: Light behaves as a **wave** when it travels and spreads (interference, diffraction, polarisation) and as a stream of **particles** when it exchanges energy and momentum with matter (photoelectric effect). Neither picture alone describes every experiment: radiation has a **dual nature**.

rows: Photoelectric effect (photons of energy hf, momentum h/λ)
Definite charge and mass; tracks; deflection in fields

visual.alt: Table showing that both light and electrons display wave behaviour in some experiments and particle behaviour in others

slides.narration: So is light a wave or a stream of particles? Experiments on how it travels, such as interference and diffraction, need the wave picture. Experiments on how it gives up energy, such as the photoelectric effect, need photons. Neither picture alone covers everything. Light has a dual nature, and as we shall see, so do electrons.

slides.heading: de Broglie’s hypothesis
slides.body_md:
In 1924 de Broglie proposed that nature is symmetric: if waves can behave as particles, **moving particles should behave as waves**. A particle of momentum $p$ has a wavelength
$$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{mv}$$
bullets: The same relation as for a photon, read the other way round.
Larger momentum, shorter wavelength.
For everyday objects λ is far too small to detect.

visual.alt: Table comparing de Broglie wavelengths: an electron accelerated through 240 volts has a wavelength of 79 picometres, comparable to atomic spacings, while a sprinter or a bullet has a wavelength far too small to detect

slides.narration: De Broglie suggested that the link between waves and particles works both ways. If light waves can act as particles with momentum h over lambda, then a moving particle should have a wave whose wavelength is h divided by its momentum. A heavier or faster particle has a shorter wavelength. For a sprinter or a bullet the wavelength is absurdly small, which is why we never notice it.

slides.heading: Electrons accelerated through a potential difference
slides.body_md:
An electron accelerated from rest through V gains $K = eV = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$, so $p = \sqrt{2meV}$ and
$$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}} = \dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{2 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,V}} \approx \dfrac{1.22}{\sqrt{V}}\ \text{nm}$$
bullets: A particle of charge q and mass m: λ = h/√(2mqV).
Quadrupling V halves λ.

visual.alt: Graph of the de Broglie wavelength of an electron, in picometres, against the potential difference that accelerated it, from 20 to 1000 volts: the wavelength falls steeply at first and then slowly, as one over the square root of the voltage, to 79 picometres at 240 volts, comparable to the spacing of atoms in a crystal
visual.caption: λ = h/√(2meV) ≈ 1.22/√V nm with h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.

slides.narration: An electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference V gains kinetic energy e V. Its momentum is the square root of two m e V, so its wavelength is h divided by that. Putting in the numbers gives about one point two two nanometres divided by the square root of the voltage. A few hundred volts gives wavelengths below a tenth of a nanometre, like X rays.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: an electron through 240 V
slides.body_md: An electron is accelerated from rest through 240 V. Find its speed, its momentum and its de Broglie wavelength.
bullets: $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2eV}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 240}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}} \approx 9.19 \times 10^{6}$ m s⁻¹.
$p = mv \approx 8.36 \times 10^{-24}$ kg m s⁻¹.
$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} \approx 7.89 \times 10^{-11}$ m $\approx 78.9$ pm; check: $\dfrac{1.22}{\sqrt{240}} \approx 0.079$ nm.

slides.narration: The electron gains two hundred and forty electronvolts and reaches about nine million metres per second. Its momentum is about eight point four times ten to the minus twenty four kilogram metres per second, and its wavelength is h divided by that, about seventy nine picometres. That is close to the spacing of atoms in a crystal, which is exactly what is needed to see electrons diffract.

bullets: The regular rows of atoms in the crystal act like a diffraction grating for waves of wavelength comparable to their spacing.

A detector that could swing around the crystal counted the electrons scattered at each angle. The rows of atoms in a crystal are spaced at about the wavelength de Broglie predicted, so if electrons were waves, the crystal should diffract them.

slides.heading: What they found
slides.body_md: At most voltages the scattered intensity changed smoothly with angle. But at **54 V** a sharp **peak** appeared at a scattering angle of about **50°**, growing and then fading as V was raised past 54 V.
bullets: A peak in one direction is exactly what diffraction of waves by a crystal produces.
The wavelength found from the crystal agreed closely with h/p: electrons behave as waves.

slides.narration: For most voltages the number of scattered electrons changed smoothly with angle. But near fifty four volts a strong spur appeared at about fifty degrees, and it faded again at higher and lower voltages. A strong beam in one particular direction is the signature of diffraction by a crystal. The wavelength worked out from the crystal agreed with de Broglie’s formula: electrons really do behave as waves.

slides.heading: Electron diffraction rings
slides.body_md: G. P. Thomson sent fast electrons through a **thin metal foil** made of many tiny crystals. The screen showed **concentric rings**, just like the X-ray diffraction rings from the same foil.
bullets: Raising the accelerating voltage shortens λ and makes the rings smaller.
Electron microscopes use these very short wavelengths to resolve detail far finer than light can.

sections.heading: 1. The photoelectric effect: observations and experimental facts
sections.body_md:
- **Photoelectric effect:** emission of electrons (photoelectrons) from a metal surface when light of suitable frequency falls on it.
- **Hertz (1887):** ultraviolet light from a transmitter spark made sparks jump more easily across a receiver gap; glass (which absorbs ultraviolet) weakened the effect, quartz did not. **Hallwachs:** a negatively charged zinc plate in ultraviolet loses its charge.
- **Lenard’s apparatus:** emitter C and collector A in an evacuated bulb, light through a quartz window, a potential divider with a reversing key to set the collector potential V, a microammeter for the photocurrent.
- **Facts:** (i) photocurrent ∝ intensity (frequency fixed, above threshold); (ii) the current saturates at large positive V and falls to zero at a negative **stopping potential** −V₀, with $eV_0 = K_{\max}$; (iii) V₀ does not depend on intensity but rises linearly with frequency; (iv) no emission below a **threshold frequency** f₀ of the metal, however intense the light; (v) emission is instantaneous (within about 10⁻⁹ s).
- **Wave theory fails:** it spreads energy over the wavefront at a rate set by intensity, so it expects K_max to grow with intensity, emission at any frequency if bright enough, and a measurable delay in dim light. Only fact (i) agrees.

key_terms.definition_md: The negative potential of the collector, relative to the emitter, that just reduces the photocurrent to zero; eV₀ equals the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.
The largest photocurrent for a given beam, reached when every emitted electron is collected; it is proportional to the intensity.

sections.heading: 2. Photons and Einstein’s photoelectric equation
sections.body_md:
- **Quantisation of radiation:** light of frequency f travels and is absorbed as **photons**, each of energy $E = hf = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$ (Planck, Einstein). Here $h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34}$ J s, so $E\,(\text{eV}) = \dfrac{1237.5}{\lambda\,(\text{nm})}$. Intensity = photons per second per unit area × hf.
- **Work function W₀:** the least energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of a metal (a few eV; depends on the metal and its surface).
- **Einstein’s equation:** one photon is absorbed by one electron; $K_{\max} = hf - W_0 = eV_0$. Electrons from deeper levels leave with less energy.
- **Threshold:** $hf_0 = W_0$, so $f_0 = \dfrac{W_0}{h}$ and $\lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{W_0}$. No emission for f < f₀ (λ > λ₀).
- **Explains the facts:** threshold (one photon must supply W₀); K_max set by f, not intensity; no delay (the whole photon is absorbed at once); current ∝ number of photons ∝ intensity.
- A graph of K_max against f is a straight line of slope h, cutting the f axis at f₀ and (extended) the K_max axis at −W₀.

key_terms.definition_md: A quantum of electromagnetic radiation of energy hf and momentum h/λ, travelling at c, with zero rest mass and no charge.
The minimum energy needed to free an electron from the surface of a metal.
The lowest frequency of light that can eject photoelectrons from a given metal: f₀ = W₀/h.

sections.heading: 3. Planck’s constant from the V₀–f graph; photon momentum
sections.body_md:
- Dividing Einstein’s equation by e: $V_0 = \dfrac{h}{e}f - \dfrac{W_0}{e}$. A graph of V₀ against f is a **straight line**: slope $\dfrac{h}{e}$ (the same for all metals, so the lines are parallel), intercept on the f axis $f_0$, intercept on the V₀ axis $-\dfrac{W_0}{e}$.
- **To find h:** measure V₀ for several frequencies, draw the best line, $h = e \times$ slope; then $W_0 = hf_0$. With h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s the slope is 4.125 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s.
- **Photon momentum:** with zero rest mass, $E = pc$, so $p = \dfrac{E}{c} = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}$. A beam of power P absorbed by a surface exerts force P/c; reflected normally, 2P/c.

key_terms.definition_md: p = h/λ = E/c: the momentum carried by a photon of wavelength λ.

sections.heading: 4. Wave–particle duality and de Broglie waves
sections.body_md:
- **Dual nature of radiation:** light shows wave behaviour in propagation (interference, diffraction, polarisation) and particle behaviour in interaction with matter (photoelectric effect).
- **de Broglie hypothesis (1924):** every moving particle has a wave associated with it, of wavelength $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{mv}$.
- **Electron accelerated from rest through V:** $eV = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$, so $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}} \approx \dfrac{1.22}{\sqrt{V}}$ nm (with h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s). In general $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$.
- Everyday objects have wavelengths far too small to show diffraction; electrons of a few hundred eV have λ ≈ 0.1 nm, comparable to atomic spacings.

key_terms.definition_md: The wavelength h/p of the wave associated with a moving particle of momentum p.
The fact that radiation and matter each show wave behaviour in some experiments and particle behaviour in others.

visual.alt: Graph of the de Broglie wavelength of an electron, in picometres, against the potential difference that accelerated it, from 20 to 1000 volts: the wavelength falls steeply at first and then slowly, as one over the square root of the voltage, to 79 picometres at 240 volts, comparable to the spacing of atoms in a crystal
visual.caption: λ = h/√(2meV) ≈ 1.22/√V nm with h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.

sections.heading: 5. Electron diffraction and the Davisson–Germer experiment (qualitative)
sections.body_md:
- **Apparatus:** an electron gun (heated filament, anode at accelerating potential V) sends a narrow beam onto a **nickel crystal** in a vacuum chamber; a **movable detector** measures the number of electrons scattered at each angle φ to the incident beam.
- **Observation:** a sharp peak (spur) in the scattered intensity at φ ≈ 50° when V = 54 V; the peak weakens at higher and lower voltages.
- **Conclusion:** a strong beam in one direction is diffraction by the regular rows of atoms; the wavelength found agreed with h/p. Electrons behave as waves, confirming de Broglie’s hypothesis.
- **Thomson:** electrons through a thin foil of tiny crystals give concentric rings like X-rays; higher V gives smaller rings.
- The quantitative treatment of the experiment is not in the ISC syllabus.

key_terms.definition_md: The spreading of an electron beam into definite directions (spots or rings) by the regular arrangement of atoms in a crystal, showing the wave nature of electrons.

cards.front_md: What did Hertz notice about his receiver gap in 1887?
cards.back_md: It sparked more easily when ultraviolet light from the transmitter spark fell on it.

cards.front_md: Why did a glass sheet weaken Hertz’s effect but quartz did not?
cards.back_md: Glass absorbs ultraviolet; quartz transmits it.

cards.front_md: Why is a photocell bulb evacuated?
cards.back_md: So photoelectrons reach the collector without colliding with gas molecules.

cards.front_md: What is the saturation current?
cards.back_md: The largest photocurrent, when all emitted electrons reach the collector; ∝ intensity.

cards.front_md: Define stopping potential.
cards.back_md: The negative collector potential that just stops the fastest photoelectrons: eV₀ = K_max.

cards.front_md: Effect of doubling intensity (same frequency) on V₀?
cards.back_md: None: V₀ is unchanged; only the current doubles.

cards.front_md: Why does some current flow at zero collector potential?
cards.back_md: Photoelectrons leave the emitter with kinetic energy and some reach the collector unaided.

cards.front_md: Three facts the wave theory cannot explain?
cards.back_md: Threshold frequency; K_max independent of intensity; no time lag.

cards.front_md: Energy of a photon?
cards.back_md: $E = hf = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$.

cards.front_md: Photon energy in eV from λ in nm (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)?
Einstein’s photoelectric equation?
Define work function.
cards.back_md: The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from a metal surface.

cards.front_md: Threshold frequency and wavelength?
cards.back_md: f₀ = W₀/h; λ₀ = hc/W₀.

cards.front_md: Why is it called the maximum kinetic energy?
cards.back_md: Electrons from deeper levels lose more energy getting out; only the topmost leave with hf − W₀.

cards.front_md: 412.5 nm photon energy?
Magnesium (W₀ = 3.7 eV) in 225 nm light: K_max?
Why no time lag in photoemission?
cards.back_md: Each photon gives all its energy to one electron at once.

cards.front_md: Slope of a V₀–f graph?
cards.back_md: h/e (4.125 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s), the same for all metals.

cards.front_md: What does the f-axis intercept of a V₀–f line give?
cards.back_md: The threshold frequency f₀; W₀ = hf₀.

cards.front_md: V₀-axis intercept of the extended V₀–f line?
cards.back_md: −W₀/e.

cards.front_md: Momentum of a photon?
cards.back_md: $p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda} = \dfrac{E}{c}$.

cards.front_md: Force of a beam of power P fully absorbed?
cards.back_md: P/c (2P/c if reflected straight back).

cards.front_md: What is meant by wave–particle duality?
cards.back_md: Radiation and matter show wave behaviour in some experiments and particle behaviour in others.

cards.front_md: de Broglie relation?
cards.back_md: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{mv}$.

cards.front_md: λ of an electron accelerated through V?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}} \approx \dfrac{1.22}{\sqrt V}$ nm.

cards.front_md: Why don’t we see a sprinter diffract?
cards.back_md: λ = h/mv ≈ 10⁻³⁶ m, far smaller than any opening.

cards.front_md: What did Davisson and Germer fire at a nickel crystal?
cards.back_md: A narrow beam of electrons accelerated through a known potential.

cards.front_md: Davisson–Germer key observation?
cards.back_md: A sharp peak in scattered electrons at about 50° for 54 V.

cards.front_md: Conclusion of the Davisson–Germer experiment?
cards.back_md: Electrons are diffracted by crystals: they behave as waves, with λ = h/p.

cards.front_md: Exam tip: K_max in eV and V₀ in volts?
cards.back_md: Same number: V₀ = 1.8 V means K_max = 1.8 eV.

questions.stem_md: In one of Hertz’s experiments, the longest spark the receiver gap could produce became shorter when a sheet of ordinary glass was placed between the transmitter spark and the receiver gap, but not when a sheet of quartz was used instead. The most reasonable conclusion is that

options.text_md: the glass sheet absorbs the radio waves travelling to the receiver
visible light from the transmitter spark heats the receiver electrodes
ultraviolet light from the transmitter spark helps charge to escape from the receiver electrodes
quartz conducts electricity and so completes the receiver circuit

questions.solution_md: Glass absorbs ultraviolet but lets visible light and radio waves through, while quartz transmits ultraviolet. Only blocking the ultraviolet weakened the receiver sparks, so ultraviolet light was helping charges leave the receiver electrodes — the first sign of the photoelectric effect — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In Lenard’s apparatus the collector is joined to the emitter through the microammeter alone, so that there is no potential difference between them. With ultraviolet light on the emitter, the microammeter still shows a small current because

options.text_md: the ultraviolet light ionises gas molecules between the plates
the light charges the collector positively
some photoelectrons leave the emitter with enough kinetic energy to reach the collector unaided
photoelectrons are pulled out of the emitter by the microammeter

questions.solution_md: Photoelectrons are emitted with kinetic energies from zero up to K_max; those moving towards the collector reach it even with no accelerating field, so a small current flows at V = 0 (the bulb is evacuated, so there is no gas to ionise) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Two curves P and Q of photocurrent against collector potential are recorded for one photocell. Both fall to zero at the same negative potential, but P levels off at three times the current of Q. Compared with the light used for Q, the light used for P has

options.text_md: three times the frequency and the same intensity
a higher frequency and a lower intensity
the same frequency and three times the intensity
the same intensity and a longer wavelength

questions.solution_md: The same stopping potential means the same K_max = hf − W₀, so the same frequency. A saturation current three times as large means three times as many photoelectrons per second, so three times the intensity — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A photocell lit by a small ultraviolet lamp is moved from 0.50 m to 1.0 m away from the lamp. Its stopping potential stays the same, while its saturation current falls to about a quarter.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. The frequency of the light is unchanged, so V₀ (set by hf − W₀) is unchanged. The intensity from a small source falls as 1/r², so doubling the distance gives a quarter of the photons per second and about a quarter of the saturation current.

questions.stem_md: In Lenard’s experiment the collector is made more and more negative relative to the emitter until the microammeter just reads zero. The magnitude of this collector potential is called the ___ potential.
questions.solution_md: The stopping (cut-off) potential V₀: at this potential even the fastest photoelectrons are turned back, so eV₀ = K_max.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When the collector of a photocell is made slightly negative, the photocurrent falls but does not become zero at once.

**Reason (R):** Photoelectrons leave the emitter with kinetic energies ranging from zero up to a maximum value.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true and R explains A: a small retarding potential turns back only the slower electrons; the current reaches zero only when the potential stops the fastest ones (eV₀ = K_max) — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Photoelectrons are emitted without any measurable delay, even when light just above the threshold frequency is very dim.

**Reason (R):** In the wave theory, the energy of light is spread continuously over the whole wavefront.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but R does not explain A: a continuous spread of energy would make each electron wait to gather enough, predicting a delay. A is explained by photons, each absorbed whole by one electron — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The saturation photocurrent of the photocell in a light meter is 4.8 μA. How many photoelectrons leave its emitter each second? Give the answer in units of 10¹³.
questions.solution_md: At saturation every emitted electron is collected: $n = \dfrac{I}{e} = \dfrac{4.8 \times 10^{-6}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 3.0 \times 10^{13}$ per second, so $\dfrac{n}{10^{13}} = 3.0$.

questions.stem_md: The fastest photoelectrons from a barium emitter are just stopped when the collector is 0.91 V below the emitter. Find their speed, in units of 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (3 significant figures). (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.)

A physicist in 1900 argues that a metal plate 3.0 m from a 1.0 W ultraviolet source will start emitting electrons only after a delay. Assume the source radiates uniformly in all directions, each electron absorbs the energy falling on an area of 2.0 × 10⁻²⁰ m², and the metal’s work function is 3.0 eV. Estimate the delay the wave theory predicts, and evaluate the argument in the light of experiment.

answer.model_answer_md:
Intensity at 3.0 m: $I = \dfrac{P}{4\pi r^2} = \dfrac{1.0}{4\pi \times 3.0^2} \approx 8.84 \times 10^{-3}$ W m⁻². Power reaching one electron: $IA \approx 1.77 \times 10^{-22}$ W. Energy needed: $3.0 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 4.8 \times 10^{-19}$ J, so $t \approx \dfrac{4.8 \times 10^{-19}}{1.77 \times 10^{-22}} \approx 2700$ s, about 45 minutes.
The argument fails: experiment shows emission within about $10^{-9}$ s, however weak the light (above threshold). Energy arrives in photons, each absorbed whole by one electron, so there is no waiting.

questions.solution_md: I = P/4πr², power on the area, time = W₀/(power); compare with the observed instantaneous emission.

marking_scheme.step: I ≈ 8.84 × 10⁻³ W m⁻² and power ≈ 1.77 × 10⁻²² W on the area
Observed emission is instantaneous; photons explain it, so the argument is rejected

questions.stem_md: Describe Lenard’s arrangement for studying the photoelectric effect, and explain how it is used to measure the stopping potential for light of a given frequency.

answer.model_answer_md: Two metal plates, an emitter C and a collector A, are sealed in an evacuated glass bulb with a quartz window, through which monochromatic light falls on C. A battery across a rheostat, with a reversing key, applies a variable potential V between A and C, read on a voltmeter; a microammeter measures the photocurrent. To find the stopping potential, the key is reversed so that A is negative, and the retarding potential is raised until the photocurrent just becomes zero; that potential is V₀.

questions.solution_md: Evacuated bulb, emitter, collector, quartz window, potential divider with reversing key, meters; increase the retarding potential until the current is zero.

marking_scheme.step: Evacuated bulb with emitter and collector; light through a quartz window
Potential divider with reversing key, voltmeter and microammeter
Collector made negative and the potential raised until the current just becomes zero: V₀

questions.stem_md: A student doubles the brightness of a lamp shining on a photocell and expects the stopping potential to double, because “twice the energy arrives each second”. Evaluate this expectation.

answer.model_answer_md: The expectation is wrong. Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons arriving per second, but each photon still carries the same energy hf. Each electron absorbs one photon, so K_max = hf − W₀ and the stopping potential are unchanged; only the number of photoelectrons, and so the saturation current, doubles.

questions.solution_md: Intensity changes the number of photons, not their energy.

marking_scheme.step: Each photon still has energy hf, so K_max and V₀ are unchanged
Twice the photons: twice the photoelectrons and saturation current

questions.stem_md: Two beams of equal intensity (the same power per unit area), of wavelengths 480 nm and 240 nm, fall in turn on the same rubidium emitter (W₀ = 2.1 eV). Assuming each photon has the same chance of freeing an electron, which beam gives (a) the larger saturation current, (b) the larger stopping potential? Explain. (hc = 1237.5 eV nm.)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The 480 nm beam. Its photons carry half the energy ($2.58$ eV against $5.16$ eV), so at equal intensity twice as many photons arrive per second, freeing twice as many electrons.
(b) The 240 nm beam: $V_0 = 5.16 - 2.1 \approx 3.06$ V, against $2.58 - 2.1 \approx 0.48$ V for 480 nm.

questions.solution_md: Equal power: N ∝ λ; V₀ = hc/λe − W₀/e.

marking_scheme.step: (a) 480 nm: half the photon energy, so twice as many photons and twice the current

questions.stem_md: (a) Describe, with a labelled diagram (described in words), Lenard’s apparatus for studying the photoelectric effect. [2] (b) Describe how the photocurrent varies with the collector potential for two beams of the same frequency but different intensities, and state what the graphs show about the stopping potential. [2] (c) For one beam the photocurrent just becomes zero when the collector is 1.25 V negative with respect to the emitter. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons in eV and in joules. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) An evacuated glass bulb contains a metal emitter C and a collector A. Monochromatic light enters through a quartz window (which transmits ultraviolet) and falls on C. A battery connected across a rheostat (potential divider) with a reversing key applies a variable potential V to A relative to C, measured by a voltmeter; a microammeter in series with A measures the photocurrent.
(b) For each beam a current flows even at V = 0. As V is made positive the current rises to a saturation value, larger for the more intense beam (saturation current ∝ intensity). As V is made negative the current falls and becomes zero at $V = -V_0$; both curves reach zero at the **same** stopping potential, so V₀ (and K_max) does not depend on intensity.
(c) $K_{\max} = eV_0 = 1.25$ eV $= 1.25 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 2.0 \times 10^{-19}$ J.

questions.solution_md: Apparatus; current–potential curves for two intensities; K_max = eV₀.

marking_scheme.step: Evacuated bulb, emitter and collector, quartz window
Potential divider with reversing key; voltmeter and microammeter
Same stopping potential for both intensities

questions.stem_md: An ultraviolet LED used to check banknotes emits light of wavelength 375 nm. Each of its photons carries an energy of about (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

options.text_md: 5.3 eV
3.3 eV
2.2 eV

questions.solution_md: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{375 \times 10^{-9}} = 5.28 \times 10^{-19}$ J, which is $\dfrac{5.28 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 3.3$ eV — option (b). (5.3 is the energy in units of 10⁻¹⁹ J, not in eV.)

questions.stem_md: Light of wavelength 540 nm from a green LED falls in turn on four clean plates with work functions: rubidium 2.1 eV, calcium 2.9 eV, aluminium 4.1 eV and platinum 5.6 eV. Taking hc = 1237.5 eV nm, photoelectrons are emitted from

options.text_md: rubidium only
all four plates
rubidium and calcium only
none of the plates

questions.solution_md: $E = \dfrac{1237.5}{540} \approx 2.29$ eV. Only rubidium has a work function below this, so only rubidium emits — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A graph of the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons (y-axis) against the frequency of the incident light (x-axis) is drawn for a calcium surface. The graph is

options.text_md: a straight line of slope h that cuts the frequency axis at the threshold frequency
a straight line through the origin of slope h
a curve that rises steeply and then levels off
a straight line of slope h/e that cuts the frequency axis at the threshold frequency

questions.solution_md: K_max = hf − W₀: a straight line of slope h, zero at f₀ = W₀/h (and, extended, −W₀ at f = 0). The slope h/e belongs to the stopping potential graph — option (a).

questions.stem_md: For a strontium photocathode lit by ultraviolet light, which single change would increase the stopping potential?

options.text_md: Using a brighter lamp of the same wavelength
Using light of a shorter wavelength
Moving the lamp closer to the photocell
Making the collector more positive

questions.solution_md: eV₀ = hc/λ − W₀ rises only if the photon energy rises, i.e. for a shorter wavelength. Brightness and distance change only the number of photons; the collector potential does not change the electrons’ energy at emission — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Graphs of maximum kinetic energy against frequency are drawn on the same axes for barium (W₀ = 2.5 eV) and for a second metal of work function 5.0 eV. Compared with the barium line, the line for the second metal

options.text_md: is twice as steep and starts at the same frequency
is parallel to it and cuts the frequency axis at half the frequency
is half as steep and starts at twice the frequency
is parallel to it and cuts the frequency axis at twice the frequency

questions.solution_md: K_max = hf − W₀: the slope h is the same for every metal, so the lines are parallel; the threshold f₀ = W₀/h doubles when W₀ doubles — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The work function of strontium is 2.6 eV. Find its threshold wavelength, in nm (3 significant figures). (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.solution_md: $hc = 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8} = 1.98 \times 10^{-25}$ J m and $W_0 = 2.6 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 4.16 \times 10^{-19}$ J, so $\lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{W_0} = \dfrac{1.98 \times 10^{-25}}{4.16 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 4.76 \times 10^{-7}$ m, that is $\lambda_0 = 476$ nm.

marking_scheme.step: λ₀ = hc/W₀ with W₀ in joules

questions.stem_md: The work function of tungsten is 4.5 eV. Find its threshold frequency, in units of 10¹⁵ Hz (3 significant figures). (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.)
questions.solution_md: $f_0 = \dfrac{W_0}{h} = \dfrac{4.5 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{6.6 \times 10^{-34}} \approx 1.09 \times 10^{15}$ Hz, i.e. 1.09 in units of $10^{15}$ Hz.

questions.stem_md: Ultraviolet light of wavelength 210 nm falls on a clean copper surface (W₀ = 4.7 eV). Find the stopping potential, in volts (2 significant figures). (Take hc = 1237.5 eV nm.)
questions.solution_md: $E = \dfrac{1237.5}{210} \approx 5.89$ eV, so $K_{\max} \approx 5.89 - 4.7 = 1.19$ eV and $V_0 \approx 1.2$ V.

questions.stem_md: Light of wavelength 275 nm ejects photoelectrons from a metal surface, and the stopping potential is found to be 1.6 V. Find the work function of the metal, in eV (2 significant figures). (Take hc = 1237.5 eV nm.)

Photons of energy 3.0 eV free electrons from a surface with a maximum kinetic energy of 0.80 eV. The wavelength of the light is now halved. Find the new maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, in eV.
questions.solution_md: Work function: $W_0 = 3.0 - 0.80 = 2.2$ eV. Halving λ doubles the photon energy to 6.0 eV, so $K_{\max} = 6.0 - 2.2 = 3.8$ eV (almost five times as much, not twice).

questions.stem_md: A 12 mW ultraviolet LED of wavelength 365 nm shines all its light on the emitter of a photocell. If one photon in every 200 frees an electron, and every freed electron is collected, find the photocurrent, in μA (3 significant figures). (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.solution_md: Photon energy $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1.98 \times 10^{-25}}{365 \times 10^{-9}} \approx 5.42 \times 10^{-19}$ J. Photons per second $N = \dfrac{P}{E} \approx 2.21 \times 10^{16}$. Electrons per second $\approx 1.11 \times 10^{14}$, so $I \approx 1.11 \times 10^{14} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \approx 1.77 \times 10^{-5}$ A, that is 17.7 μA.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons from a given metal is directly proportional to the frequency of the incident light.

**Reason (R):** Each photon of frequency f carries energy hf.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true, but A is false: K_max = hf − W₀ increases linearly with f but is not proportional to it (it is zero at f₀, not at f = 0) — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A metal lit by light above its threshold frequency emits photoelectrons even when the light is extremely weak.

**Reason (R):** The number of photoelectrons emitted per second does not depend on the intensity of the light.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: even a few photons above threshold can each free an electron at once. R is false: the number of photoelectrons per second is proportional to the intensity — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Each photon from a 1 kW infrared heater carries less energy than each photon from a 1 mW violet laser pointer.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Photon energy hf depends only on frequency; infrared has a lower frequency than violet. The heater’s much larger power comes from emitting vastly more photons, not more energetic ones.

questions.stem_md: True or false? When the wavelength of the light falling on a photoemissive surface is halved (the light still being above threshold), the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons more than doubles.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Halving λ doubles the photon energy: the new K_max = 2hf − W₀ = 2(hf − W₀) + W₀, which is twice the old K_max plus W₀.

questions.stem_md: Light of wavelength longer than 476 nm cannot free electrons from strontium however bright it is; for strontium, 476 nm is the ___ wavelength.
questions.solution_md: The threshold (cut-off) wavelength λ₀ = hc/W₀: longer wavelengths have photons with less energy than the work function.

questions.stem_md: Match each quantity for a magnesium photocell in Column A with what it depends on, in Column B.

options.text_md: Energy of each incident photon
Work function
Saturation photocurrent (frequency fixed)
Maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons

match_right.text_md: The metal and the state of its surface
Both the frequency of the light and the metal
The frequency of the light only

questions.solution_md: hf depends on f only; W₀ is a property of the surface; the saturation current counts photons, so it follows intensity; K_max = hf − W₀ depends on both f and the metal.

questions.stem_md: A faint violet lamp (about 410 nm) makes a calcium plate (W₀ = 2.9 eV) emit electrons at once, while a powerful red lamp (about 680 nm) frees none. Explain both observations using the photon model. (hc = 1237.5 eV nm.)

answer.model_answer_md: Violet photons carry $\dfrac{1237.5}{410} \approx 3.02$ eV, more than W₀ = 2.9 eV, so each absorbed photon can free an electron at once, however few photons arrive. Red photons carry only $\approx 1.82$ eV, less than W₀; an electron absorbs one photon at a time, so no number of red photons can free it.

questions.solution_md: Compare photon energy with W₀; one photon per electron.

marking_scheme.step: Violet photon ≈ 3.02 eV > 2.9 eV: emission at once even in faint light
Red photon ≈ 1.82 eV < 2.9 eV: no emission however bright, one photon per electron

questions.stem_md: For barium (W₀ = 2.5 eV): (a) find the threshold wavelength; (b) state, with a reason, whether yellow light of wavelength 560 nm can eject photoelectrons from it. (hc = 1237.5 eV nm.)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{W_0} = \dfrac{1237.5}{2.5} = 495$ nm.
(b) No: 560 nm is longer than the threshold wavelength of 495 nm, so each photon has only $\dfrac{1237.5}{560} \approx 2.21$ eV, less than the work function of 2.5 eV.

questions.solution_md: λ₀ = hc/W₀; compare.

questions.stem_md: When light of wavelength 280 nm falls on a metal surface, the stopping potential is 1.32 V. Find (a) the work function of the metal, (b) its threshold wavelength, (c) the stopping potential for light of wavelength 230 nm. (hc = 1237.5 eV nm.)
questions.solution_md: W₀ = hc/λ − eV₀; λ₀ = hc/W₀; then V₀ for the new wavelength.

questions.stem_md: For a given photoemissive surface, describe the shape of each graph and give the reason in each case: (a) saturation photocurrent against intensity of light of fixed frequency; (b) stopping potential against intensity; (c) maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons against frequency.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) A straight line through the origin: the number of photons, and so of photoelectrons, per second is proportional to the intensity. (b) A horizontal straight line: the stopping potential depends on the energy of each photon, not on how many arrive. (c) A straight line of slope h, starting at the threshold frequency f₀ on the frequency axis (no emission below it), because K_max = hf − W₀.

questions.solution_md: Current ∝ intensity; V₀ independent of intensity; K_max linear in f with intercept f₀.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Straight line through the origin, with reason
(c) Straight line of slope h from f₀, with reason

questions.stem_md: (a) What is meant by the work function of a metal and by its threshold frequency? Write Einstein’s photoelectric equation in terms of them. [1] (b) Use the photon picture to explain why (i) there is a threshold frequency, (ii) emission begins without delay. [2] (c) Calcium has a work function of 2.9 eV. Light of wavelength 248 nm falls on it. Find (i) the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons in eV, (ii) their maximum speed. [2] (hc = 1237.5 eV nm, mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The work function W₀ is the least energy needed to remove an electron from the metal surface; the threshold frequency f₀ is the lowest frequency that can eject photoelectrons, with $hf_0 = W_0$. Einstein’s equation: $K_{\max} = hf - W_0 = h(f - f_0)$.
(b)(i) An electron absorbs one whole photon. If $hf < W_0$ it cannot escape, however many photons arrive, so emission needs $f \geq f_0$. (ii) The photon gives all its energy to one electron at once; there is no gradual build-up, so emission starts without delay.
(c)(i) $E = \dfrac{1237.5}{248} \approx 4.99$ eV, so $K_{\max} \approx 4.99 - 2.9 = 2.09$ eV.
(ii) $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 2.09 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}} \approx 8.57 \times 10^{5}$ m s⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; one photon per electron; K_max = hc/λ − W₀; v = √(2K/m).

marking_scheme.step: Threshold: one photon must supply W₀
No delay: whole photon absorbed at once

questions.stem_md: A student plots the stopping potential V₀ (y-axis) against the frequency f (x-axis) for a photocathode and gets a straight line. Multiplying the slope of this line by the electronic charge e gives

options.text_md: Planck’s constant h
the work function of the photocathode
the threshold frequency of the photocathode
the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons

questions.solution_md: V₀ = (h/e)f − W₀/e, so the slope is h/e and e × slope = h — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The straight line of stopping potential against frequency for a metal, extended back to zero frequency, meets the stopping-potential axis at −W₀/e.

**Reason (R):** The slope of this line is h/e for every metal.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true: putting f = 0 in V₀ = (h/e)f − W₀/e gives −W₀/e, and the slope h/e is universal. But the slope being the same for all metals does not explain the value of the intercept — option (b).

questions.stem_md: For a photocathode, light of frequency 7.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz gives a stopping potential of 0.62 V and light of frequency 1.15 × 10¹⁵ Hz gives 2.27 V. Find Planck’s constant from these readings, in units of 10⁻³⁴ J s (2 significant figures). (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.)

For a photocathode, light of frequency 7.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz gives a stopping potential of 0.62 V and light of frequency 1.15 × 10¹⁵ Hz gives 2.27 V. Without assuming a value of h, find the work function of the photocathode, in eV (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: The line has slope $\dfrac{h}{e} = \dfrac{2.27 - 0.62}{4.0 \times 10^{14}} = 4.125 \times 10^{-15}$ V s. At $f = 7.5 \times 10^{14}$ Hz: $\dfrac{hf}{e} = 4.125 \times 10^{-15} \times 7.5 \times 10^{14} \approx 3.094$ V, so $\dfrac{W_0}{e} = 3.094 - 0.62 = 2.474$ V, giving $W_0 \approx 2.47$ eV (threshold $f_0 = \dfrac{W_0}{h} \approx 6.0 \times 10^{14}$ Hz).

marking_scheme.step: Slope h/e from the two readings

questions.stem_md: Find the momentum of a photon of ultraviolet light of wavelength 220 nm, in units of 10⁻²⁷ kg m s⁻¹. (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.)

questions.stem_md: A 3.0 W laser beam falls normally on a black surface that absorbs it completely. Using the momentum carried by the photons, find the force on the surface, in units of 10⁻⁸ N. (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.)

questions.stem_md: Explain how a graph of stopping potential against frequency for a photocell can be used to find (a) Planck’s constant, (b) the work function of the emitter.

answer.model_answer_md: Einstein’s equation gives V₀ = (h/e)f − W₀/e, a straight line. (a) Measure V₀ for several frequencies, draw the best line and find its slope; h = e × slope. (b) The line meets the frequency axis at the threshold frequency f₀, and W₀ = hf₀ (equivalently, the line extended meets the V₀ axis at −W₀/e).

questions.stem_md: Starting from Einstein’s photoelectric equation, show that the graph of stopping potential V₀ against frequency f is a straight line. For a certain emitter the line cuts the frequency axis at 8.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz and passes through V₀ = 1.65 V at f = 1.2 × 10¹⁵ Hz. Find Planck’s constant and the work function in eV. (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.)

answer.model_answer_md:
$eV_0 = hf - W_0$ gives $V_0 = \dfrac{h}{e}f - \dfrac{W_0}{e}$: linear in f with constant slope h/e, i.e. a straight line.
Slope $= \dfrac{1.65}{(12 - 8.0) \times 10^{14}} = 4.125 \times 10^{-15}$ V s, so $h = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 4.125 \times 10^{-15} = 6.6 \times 10^{-34}$ J s.
$W_0 = hf_0 = 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 8.0 \times 10^{14} = 5.28 \times 10^{-19}$ J $= 3.3$ eV.

questions.solution_md: V₀ = (h/e)f − W₀/e; slope from intercept and one point; W₀ = hf₀.

questions.stem_md: An 8.0 mW laser of wavelength 660 nm shines normally on a small mirror that reflects all the light straight back. Find (a) the momentum of each photon, (b) the number of photons striking the mirror per second, (c) the force on the mirror. (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{660 \times 10^{-9}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-27}$ kg m s⁻¹.
(b) $E = pc = 3.0 \times 10^{-19}$ J, so $N = \dfrac{8.0 \times 10^{-3}}{3.0 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 2.67 \times 10^{16}$ s⁻¹.
(c) Each reflected photon’s momentum changes by $2p$: $F = 2Np \approx 5.33 \times 10^{-11}$ N (equal to $\dfrac{2P}{c}$).

questions.solution_md: p = h/λ; N = P/E; F = 2Np on reflection.

questions.stem_md: True or false? On a graph of stopping potential against frequency, the line for platinum (W₀ = 5.6 eV) lies to the right of the line for barium (W₀ = 2.5 eV) and is steeper.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The platinum line does start at a higher threshold frequency (to the right), but both lines have the same slope h/e: they are parallel, not steeper.

questions.stem_md: (a) Show that, according to Einstein’s equation, the stopping potential varies linearly with frequency, and state what the slope and the frequency-axis intercept of the graph represent. [2] (b) A photocell gives these readings: f = 7.0, 9.0, 11.0, 13.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz give V₀ = 0.49, 1.31, 2.14, 2.96 V respectively. Using the end points of the best straight line, find Planck’s constant. [2] (c) Find the work function of the emitter in eV. [1] (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $eV_0 = hf - W_0$, so $V_0 = \dfrac{h}{e}f - \dfrac{W_0}{e}$: a straight line. Slope $= \dfrac{h}{e}$ (the same for all metals); the intercept on the f axis is the threshold frequency $f_0 = \dfrac{W_0}{h}$.
(b) The points lie on a straight line (successive rises 0.82, 0.83, 0.82 V). Slope $= \dfrac{2.96 - 0.49}{(13 - 7) \times 10^{14}} \approx 4.12 \times 10^{-15}$ V s, so $h = e \times \text{slope} \approx 6.59 \times 10^{-34}$ J s.
(c) $f_0 = 7.0 \times 10^{14} - \dfrac{0.49}{4.12 \times 10^{-15}} \approx 5.81 \times 10^{14}$ Hz, so $W_0 = hf_0 \approx 3.83 \times 10^{-19}$ J $\approx 2.39$ eV.

questions.solution_md: V₀ = (h/e)f − W₀/e; slope from the end points; intercept → f₀, W₀ = hf₀.

made 9 times as large

options.text_md: a straight line through the origin
a rectangular hyperbola, since λp is constant
a straight line with a negative slope
a parabola opening upwards

Deflection of a beam of electrons by a magnetic field
Emission of light by a heated tungsten filament
Rings formed on a screen when a beam of electrons passes through a thin metal foil

questions.stem_md: An electron in a vacuum tube moves at 2.2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. Find its de Broglie wavelength, in nm (3 significant figures). (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg.)

questions.stem_md: Electrons accelerated from rest through 50 V and through 800 V are compared. Find the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths, λ(50 V)/λ(800 V).
questions.solution_md: $\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{V}}$, so the ratio is $\sqrt{\dfrac{800}{50}} = \sqrt{16} = 4$.

Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true and R explains A: a 1000 kg car at a few m/s has λ = h/mv of order 10⁻³⁷ m, and diffraction is noticeable only when the opening is comparable to the wavelength — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An electron and a photon that have the same wavelength also have the same energy.

**Reason (R):** An electron and a photon of the same wavelength have the same momentum, h/λ.

Choose the correct option.
