questions.stem_md: True or false? If the speed of a slow-moving electron is doubled, its de Broglie wavelength is halved.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. λ = h/(mv): for a non-relativistic electron the mass is constant, so doubling v doubles the momentum and halves λ.

questions.stem_md: Light produces an interference pattern in Young’s double-slit experiment and ejects electrons in a photocell. Explain how these two experiments together lead to the idea of the dual nature of radiation.

answer.model_answer_md: Interference needs overlapping waves from the two slits, so light travels as a wave. Photoemission needs light to deliver energy in packets hf, each absorbed whole by one electron: particle (photon) behaviour. Neither picture explains both, so radiation has a dual nature: wave-like in propagation, particle-like in interaction.

questions.solution_md: Interference → wave; photoemission → photons; together → duality.

marking_scheme.step: Interference shows wave behaviour; photoemission shows photons
Neither alone explains both: dual nature

questions.stem_md: State de Broglie’s relation. Show that the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference V is h/√(2meV), and hence that it is about 1.22/√V nm when h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

answer.model_answer_md:
A particle of momentum p has an associated wave of wavelength $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{mv}$.
Accelerated from rest through V, the electron gains $eV = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$, so $p = \sqrt{2meV}$ and $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}$.
Substituting: $\sqrt{2 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 5.40 \times 10^{-25}$, so $\lambda \approx \dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{5.40 \times 10^{-25}\sqrt{V}} \approx \dfrac{1.22 \times 10^{-9}}{\sqrt{V}}$ m, i.e. about 1.22/√V nm.

questions.solution_md: λ = h/p; eV = p²/2m; substitute constants.

questions.stem_md: An electron and a photon each have an energy of 2.0 keV. Find the wavelength of each, and say which is longer and by roughly what factor. (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg)

answer.model_answer_md:
Photon: $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{E} = \dfrac{1.98 \times 10^{-25}}{2000 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 6.19 \times 10^{-10}$ m $= 0.619$ nm.
Electron: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}} = \dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{2 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 3.2 \times 10^{-16}}} \approx 2.73 \times 10^{-11}$ m $\approx 0.0273$ nm.
The photon’s wavelength is longer, by a factor of about 23: for the same energy the electron has much more momentum.

questions.solution_md: Photon λ = hc/E; electron λ = h/√(2mK); compare.

questions.stem_md: Explain why an electron microscope using electrons accelerated through 25 kV can resolve much finer detail than a light microscope. Support your answer with the electron’s de Broglie wavelength. (Take λ ≈ 1.22/√V nm.)

answer.model_answer_md: The finest detail an instrument resolves is limited by the wavelength it uses. The electrons have $\lambda \approx \dfrac{1.22}{\sqrt{25000}} \approx 0.0077$ nm (about 7.7 pm), nearly $10^{5}$ times shorter than visible light (400–700 nm; about $6.5 \times 10^{4}$ times shorter than 500 nm green light), so the electron microscope can resolve far finer detail.

questions.solution_md: Resolution ∝ wavelength; electron λ ≈ 7.7 pm ≪ 500 nm.

marking_scheme.step: Electron λ ≈ 7.7 pm, nearly 10⁵ times shorter than light

questions.stem_md: (a) State de Broglie’s hypothesis. [1] (b) Derive an expression for the de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass m and charge q accelerated from rest through a potential difference V. [2] (c) The electrons in an old cathode-ray tube are accelerated through 1.5 kV. Find their de Broglie wavelength, in picometres. [1] (d) Explain why such electrons can be diffracted by a crystal but not noticeably by a slit 0.1 mm wide. [1] (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Every moving particle has a wave associated with it; its wavelength is $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{mv}$, where p is its momentum.
(b) Work done by the field: $qV = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$, so $p = \sqrt{2mqV}$ and $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$.
(c) $\lambda = \dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{2 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1500}} \approx 3.16 \times 10^{-11}$ m $\approx 31.6$ pm.
(d) Diffraction is noticeable only when the obstacle or opening is comparable to the wavelength. The spacing of atoms in a crystal (about 0.1–0.3 nm) is of the same order as 0.03 nm, but a 0.1 mm slit is millions of times wider, so the spreading is negligible.

questions.solution_md: λ = h/p; qV = p²/2m; substitute; compare sizes.

marking_scheme.step: Crystal spacing comparable to λ; slit far too wide

questions.stem_md: In the Davisson–Germer experiment, a sharp peak in the number of electrons scattered by the nickel crystal was found at one particular angle. This showed that

options.text_md: the electrons were knocking photoelectrons out of the nickel
the electrons were diffracted by the regular arrangement of atoms, as waves would be
the nickel nuclei repelled the electrons into one direction
the electrons lost all their kinetic energy inside the crystal

questions.solution_md: A strong scattered beam in one definite direction is the signature of diffraction by the rows of atoms in a crystal, which only waves show. The wavelength found agreed with h/p — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Davisson and Germer used a crystal, rather than a ruled diffraction grating, to diffract their electrons because

options.text_md: the spacing of atoms in a crystal is comparable to the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons
a crystal conducts electricity and so removes the charge of the electrons
electrons cannot travel through air to reach a grating
a ruled grating would absorb the electrons as photons

questions.solution_md: Diffraction is noticeable only when the spacing is comparable to the wavelength. Electrons of tens of eV have λ of about 0.1–0.2 nm, like the spacing of atoms in a crystal, while ruled gratings have spacings of about a micrometre — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the Davisson–Germer experiment, the sharp peak in scattered electrons appeared at the same angle and with the same strength for every accelerating voltage.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The peak was sharpest at 54 V, near 50°; at higher and lower voltages it weakened and shifted, because changing V changes the electrons’ wavelength.

questions.stem_md: When a beam of fast electrons passes through a thin metal foil made of many tiny crystals, the screen beyond it shows a central spot surrounded by concentric ___.
questions.solution_md: Concentric rings (circles), like the X-ray diffraction rings from the same foil: the electrons are diffracted as waves.

questions.stem_md: Match each part of the Davisson–Germer apparatus in Column A with its role in Column B.

options.text_md: Heated filament
Anode at potential V
Nickel crystal
Movable detector

match_right.text_md: Diffracts the electrons with its regular rows of atoms
Counts the electrons scattered at each angle
Accelerates the electrons and so fixes their wavelength

questions.solution_md: The filament emits electrons; the accelerating potential sets their energy and wavelength; the crystal’s atoms diffract them; the detector, swung round an arc, measures the scattered intensity at each angle.

questions.stem_md: In the Davisson–Germer experiment, why must (a) the apparatus be evacuated, and (b) all the electrons be accelerated through the same potential difference?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) In air the electrons would collide with gas molecules, lose energy and be scattered at random, hiding any diffraction peak. (b) The de Broglie wavelength depends on the electrons’ speed, which is fixed by the accelerating potential; a single potential gives a single wavelength and a sharp peak.

questions.solution_md: Vacuum avoids collisions; one V gives one wavelength.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Avoids collisions with gas molecules that scatter the electrons
(b) One potential gives one speed and so one wavelength

questions.stem_md: Electrons accelerated through a few thousand volts and X-rays of similar wavelength are sent in turn through the same thin metal foil, and both produce rings of the same size on a screen. (a) What do you conclude about the electrons? (b) How would the rings change if the accelerating potential of the electrons were increased? (c) Why does this behaviour support de Broglie’s hypothesis rather than the idea that the electrons are simply bouncing off atoms?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The electrons are diffracted by the crystals of the foil exactly as X-ray waves are, so they behave as waves with a wavelength similar to that of the X-rays. (b) A higher potential gives faster electrons with a shorter wavelength (λ = h/p), so the rings become smaller. (c) Particles bouncing off atoms would spread out smoothly; sharp rings whose size follows h/p show interference of waves, as de Broglie predicted.

questions.solution_md: Diffraction like X-rays; higher V, shorter λ, smaller rings; sharp rings need waves.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Higher V: shorter λ, smaller rings
(c) Sharp rings need wave interference; size follows h/p

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In the Davisson–Germer experiment, the electron beam had to be accelerated through a precisely known potential difference.

**Reason (R):** The kinetic energy, and hence the de Broglie wavelength, of the electrons is fixed by the accelerating potential difference.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true and R explains A: to compare the diffraction with de Broglie’s prediction, the electrons’ wavelength must be known, and it is set by eV = p²/2m — option (a).

questions.stem_md: (a) Draw (describe in words) a labelled diagram of the Davisson–Germer apparatus. [2] (b) State the main observation made with electrons accelerated through 54 V and explain how it shows the wave nature of electrons. [2] (c) Why is a crystal used rather than a narrow slit? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Inside a vacuum chamber, an electron gun — a heated filament with an anode at an accelerating potential V — sends a fine beam of electrons normally onto the face of a nickel crystal. A movable detector (collector connected to a galvanometer) can be swung round an arc centred on the crystal to measure the number of electrons scattered at each angle φ to the incident beam.
(b) The scattered intensity varied smoothly with angle except near 54 V, when a sharp peak appeared at a scattering angle of about 50°; it weakened at higher and lower voltages. A strong beam in one direction is what diffraction of waves by the regular rows of atoms produces, and the wavelength deduced agreed with de Broglie’s λ = h/p, so electrons behave as waves.
(c) Diffraction is noticeable only when the spacing is comparable to the wavelength; the atomic spacing in a crystal (about 0.1 nm) matches the electrons’ wavelength, while any slit that can be made is far too wide.

questions.solution_md: Gun, crystal, movable detector, vacuum; peak at 54 V near 50°; spacing comparable to λ.
